title: Desperado: sell a doomed piece dearly
summary: When a piece is lost anyway, make it capture or check on its way out.

steps.md:
A **desperado** is a piece that is lost anyway (attacked and unable to escape, or about to be captured in an exchange) and therefore **captures or checks as expensively as possible before it dies**. It is closely related to the zwischenzug: in a sequence of mutual captures, the side that has a doomed piece should ask "What can this piece take *before* it is taken?"

Typical situations: both sides have pieces en prise; a piece is attacked by a pawn and cannot retreat; a pinned piece will be lost, so it takes something first.

White to move. Black has just played ...Qxe4, offering a queen trade. The automatic reply is 20.Qxe4 Nxe4, equal material. But the d5-knight is attacked by the f6-knight and the black queen can take it later. Look at the *knight* first: it can capture on f6 **with check** before White recaptures the queen.

steps.prompt: White to move. Play the idea from the diagram.
steps.explain: **20.Nxf6+!** The knight takes a piece with check; after 20...Bxf6 **21.Qxe4** White has won a full knight. Had White played 20.Qxe4?! Nxe4 first, nothing would have been gained.

steps.question: Your knight is attacked by a pawn and has no safe square. What is the desperado question?
choices: Which square loses the least material?
What can the knight capture, preferably with check, before it is taken?
Can I defend the knight with another piece?
steps.explain: A doomed piece should **earn something**: a pawn, a piece, or a check that gains a tempo. Only when it can take nothing does "where does it lose least?" become the question.

steps.prompt: White to move. Black has just played ...Rxf1, attacking your knight. Kxf1 looks natural. Find the better capture first.
steps.explain: The e1-knight is attacked and Black's other rook hangs on d3. **38.Nxd3!** takes the rook first; 38...Nxd3 and only now **39.Kxf1**. White has won both rooks for a knight and is completely winning. 38.Kxf1? Rxb3 would leave Black a rook up.

steps.prompt: White to move. Black has just played ...Bxb3, attacking your d5-rook. Use the doomed rook.
steps.explain: The d5-rook is attacked, so it may as well go out with a bang: **31.Rxh5!** threatens Qh7 mate, and 31...gxh5 is forced in practice. But the g6-pawn was the only piece blocking the sixth rank: **32.Qxb6** wins the queen. A desperado rook that also clears a line.

steps.question: In a sequence of mutual captures, both sides have a piece en prise. Which rule of thumb is correct?
choices: Capture the most valuable piece first, because you might not get another chance
Count the whole sequence: a desperado capture is good only if what your piece takes is worth more than what you would otherwise lose
Always capture with check, even if it costs material
steps.explain: Desperado is **counting with intermediate moves**. List the captures available to both sides, then count the material at the end of each line. A check is valuable when it gains time, not by itself. Typical error: grabbing with the doomed piece and overlooking that the opponent has his own desperado reply.

steps.md:
**Retrieval check.** (1) Define desperado in one sentence. (2) In the ...Qxe4 example, why was 20.Qxe4 wrong? (3) What else did the doomed rook on h5 achieve besides capturing a pawn?

Answers: a doomed piece captures or checks as much as possible before being taken; it allowed Black to trade queens and keep the knights, while 20.Nxf6+ won a piece; it removed the g6-pawn from the sixth rank so the queen could capture on b6.

sources: Yusupov, Build Up Your Chess 2 (Quality Chess, 2009), chapter on desperado and intermediate moves
Dvoretsky & Yusupov, Secrets of Chess Training (Edition Olms, 1996), calculation of mutual captures
